name: Electric Blue
lede: Electric blue is a bright, saturated blue tied to the glow of electrical discharge; the name was in fashion shops by the 1870s, as a dusty periwinkle, long before it became the color of the future.

sections.title: The color of discharge
sections.body:
St Clair opens her chapter with the night of 26 April 1986 [1]. Sasha Yuvchenko, a 24-year-old engineer, came out of the wrecked Chernobyl reactor building and saw a beam of light rising from it, which he later described as bluish and beautiful [1]. The glow comes from ionized air: nitrogen and oxygen molecules are violently excited and release visible photons [1]. Sparks, lightning and St Elmo's fire, the light that dances on ships' masts, are bright blue for the same reason, sometimes tinted violet [1].

The name is also used for noctilucent clouds, which Paterson describes as electric blue cloud at high altitude that reflects sunlight at dawn or dusk [2].

sections.title: A Victorian fashion shade
sections.body: The name is older than the film images. St Clair dates a dusty periwinkle shade named electric blue to the late 1800s, when Swan and Edison were working toward electric light [1]. A British drapers' trade paper mentions dark electric blue faille and velvet in January 1874, and the *Young Ladies' Journal* notes a walking dress of electric blue nun's cloth in November 1883 [1]. St Clair calls it a periwinkle, while Paterson's dictionary says a brilliant light blue [1][2]. The books disagree on how bright it was, and the vivid swatch on this page is the modern idea, not the Victorian one [1][2].

sections.title: The color of the future
sections.body: St Clair argues that electric blue has always stood for modernity [1]. The technology in *Minority Report* (2002) is powered by it, as is the light in *Tron* (1982 and 2010), the publicity for *Inception* (2010) and the dystopian future of *WALL-E* (2008) [1]. *The Matrix* (1999) is the exception: its screens glow green, like the monochrome computer monitors it imitated, which were mostly gone by the 1980s [1]. The same chapter notes an unease in the picture, since we are drawn to this blue and a little afraid of it [1].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body: This swatch is #0652FF, a name from the xkcd color survey (2010) that our library also files under the ISCC-NBS 1955 dictionary as a strong purplish blue, 10.7 units from its block 186 [3]. It is far more saturated than a periwinkle, and it sits beside [[royal-blue]], [[dodger-blue]] and [[azure]] [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Painters in our archive almost never show this blue. No painting in our archive of 23,781 has a color within 4 units of it covering at least 1 per cent of the canvas, as photographed [4]. That describes this archive and not painting as a whole, but it fits a color that is closer to a lamp than to a pigment [4].

The word is a modern one. In printed English the phrase is first traced around 1890, begins to climb about 2000 and peaks near 2010 [4]. The 1874 trade journal shows that print can be older than the trace [1][4].

questions.q: What produces the electric blue glow that Yuvchenko saw?
The 1870s shade called electric blue was a dusty periwinkle.

openers: The first electric blue was a Victorian fashion shade: dark electric blue velvet appears in a trade paper of January 1874.
